claims.text: Atomic size mismatch primarily governs hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch impedes dislocation motion.
The alloys in the proposed comparison are homogeneous and single-phase.
The alloys have controlled, uniform chemical compositions.
Alloy composition will be varied systematically to produce different atomic size mismatches while mixing entropy and processing conditions are held constant.
Identical homogenization and quenching treatments will prevent secondary-phase formation.
Atomic size disparities generate lattice distortion.
Atomic size disparities generate additional dislocation-pinning sites.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases lattice strain.
Increased lattice strain impedes dislocation movement.
Impeded dislocation movement produces dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups increase hardness and strength.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher Vickers hardness than baseline alloys with minimal size disparity.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than baseline alloys with minimal size disparity.
High-entropy alloys composed of elements with nearly similar atomic radii have minimal lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys tested at room temperature without significant secondary phases or ordering.
At elevated temperatures or under severe deformation that promotes phase separation, mechanisms other than lattice-distortion strengthening may dominate.
Solid-solution strengthening effects or microstructural evolution may contribute concurrently to hardness and strength.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength at greater atomic size mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of a correlation between measured lattice distortion or dislocation behavior and mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.
